issues.legal_issue: A High Court may revise a revenue authority’s finding on whether the relationship that gives it jurisdiction exists when that finding leads the authority to refuse to exercise its jurisdiction.
material_facts: A person claiming to be a cultivating tenant applied to have a deposited rent amount declared correct under section 3(3) of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955.
The landowner disputed that a landlord–cultivating tenant relationship existed.
The Revenue Court found that the applicant was not a cultivating tenant and dismissed the application.
In revision, the High Court found that the tenancy existed, determined that the deposited amount was correct, and allowed the application.
The Supreme Court found no demonstrated error in the High Court’s finding that the tenancy existed.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had jurisdiction to review the Revenue Court’s finding because the existence of the landlord–cultivating tenant relationship was a preliminary fact on which the Revenue Court’s jurisdiction depended. Having found that the relationship existed, the High Court could set aside the Revenue Court’s erroneous refusal to exercise jurisdiction; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6-B of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955 deems the Revenue Divisional Officer a court subordinate to the High Court for the purposes of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Under section 115(a) and (b), the High Court may correct an erroneous assumption of jurisdiction or an erroneous refusal to exercise jurisdiction. Findings on questions that do not touch jurisdiction are not revisable under those clauses, but a decision on a preliminary fact on which jurisdiction depends is reviewable. The existence of the landlord–cultivating tenant relationship was essential to the Revenue Court’s jurisdiction under the Act, including its jurisdiction under section 3(3). No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: revision_from_subordinate_authority and no_appeal_available and statutory_revision_power_applies and relationship_is_a_preliminary_jurisdictional_fact and relationship_actually_existed and authority_found_relationship_absent_and_refused_to_act

predicates.revision_from_subordinate_authority: A party sought revision in the High Court from a decision of a subordinate authority exercising limited jurisdiction.
predicates.no_appeal_available: No appeal lay to the High Court from the subordinate authority’s decision.
predicates.statutory_revision_power_applies: A governing law made the authority’s decision subject to the High Court’s revisional jurisdiction.
predicates.relationship_is_a_preliminary_jurisdicti: The authority’s jurisdiction depended on whether a specified relationship existed between the contending parties.
predicates.relationship_actually_existed: The specified relationship between the contending parties existed.
predicates.authority_found_relationship_absent_and_: The authority found that the relationship did not exist and, on that basis, refused to exercise its jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a party seeks revision from a subordinate authority that has refused to act because it found absent a relationship on which its jurisdiction depends, and that relationship actually existed, the High Court may correct the jurisdictional refusal.
